content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's core claim — that in scriptural symbolism 'the name' is the covenant, so that to be called by God's name is to be brought into covenant relationship the way a bride takes her husband's name — is the reading that best explains the four printed texts taken together. The 2 Samuel 7 substitution (David proposes a house for 'the ark of the covenant'; God answers 'an house for my name') is a genuine textual pivot the character/person reading does not exploit. Exodus 20:7 read as 'bearing the name for emptiness' (shav) is not idiosyncratic — it matches the lexical fact that the idiom is nasa shem, to bear/carry a name, and it explains Ezekiel 36:20-23 (the name profaned by faithless conduct, hallowed by making the people holy) without any appeal to speech at all. Most decisively, Isaiah 4:1 ('only let us be called by thy name') and Ruth 3:9 (the kanaph spread over the bride, echoed in God's own wedding oath to Israel in Ezekiel 16:8, 'I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee') are marriage-covenant name-bearing texts that the mainstream 'name = character/identity of the bearer' reading handles poorly: the seven women do not want Isaiah's man's character, they want covenant standing under his name. The Numbers 15:38-39 detail (tassels on the kanaph as reminders of all the commandments) cleanly ties the printed entry's final clause to the cited Ruth text. The strongest counter (name = the person's own character, presence, and authority) explains Ex 20:7 and 2 Sam 7:13 adequately but the two bridal texts only via its own 'covenant ownership and belonging' sub-reading — which converges with, rather than defeats, the book's core. No supplied text is better explained by the counter in a way the book's core cannot absorb.","book_core_identification":"'The name' symbolically is the covenant itself — the binding relationship between God and His people — so that to bear, be called by, act in, or take the name is to own (or empty) that covenant, entered the way a bride takes her husband's name.","book_secondary_elaborations":["The bridal mechanism: being 'called by thy name' = marriage, with the husband's provision of food and raiment (Isa 4:1; Ex 21:10; Ezek 16:8-13)","The kanaph/wing identification: coming under the husband's wing whose corners carry tassels reminding of the commandments (Ruth 3:9; Num 15:38-39; Ruth 2:12; Zech 8:23)","The Angel of Exodus 23 with 'my name in him' identified as the pre-incarnate Christ (Isa 63:9; 1 Cor 10:4)","The Lord's Prayer read line-by-line as the covenant in miniature (Matt 6:9-15; Deut 8:3; Ex 16:4; Deut 15:2)","Babel's self-made name as the covenant-name's counterfeit, resolved in the two forehead-names of Revelation 13-14","Ex 6:3 resolved as covenant-entry rather than vocabulary: Abraham knew the sound but not yet the covenant the name would carry","Levirate 'raising up the name' as house-building, running Ruth 4 into the house of David and 2 Samuel 7"],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The mainstream reading (Responses A-C): a name symbolizes the essential character, identity, presence, and authority of its bearer — the name stands for the person themselves. God's 'my name' in 2 Sam 7:13 is His presence dwelling in the temple (name theology); Ex 20:7 forbids invoking or misusing what represents God's own person; Isa 4:1 and Ruth 3:9 are then explained through the 'covenant ownership and belonging' facet (Num 6:27; Isa 43:7): to be called by a name is to be claimed as belonging to the bearer.","counter_core_identification":"The name = the person who bears it (their character, being, presence, and delegated authority), not the covenant relationship as such.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The counter denies that 'the name' refers to the covenant bond itself; it holds that the name refers to the divine (or human) person — being, character, presence, authority — so that covenant belonging is at most a derived application of bearing the person's name, not the name's referent.","counter_case":["Ex 3:13-15 and Ex 34:5-7 (not printed, but central to the tradition): God reveals and 'proclaims' His name by declaring His being and attributes — name as self-disclosure of the person, not of a covenant instrument.","2 Sam 7:13 read via Deuteronomic name theology: the temple built 'for my name' houses God's localized presence (Deut 12:5, 11; 1 Kgs 8:27-29), which explains the verse without equating name and ark/covenant.","Ex 20:7 as prohibition of profaning what represents God's person — false oaths and irreverent invocation dishonor God Himself, a reading with deep traditional support.","Isa 4:1 and Ruth 3:9 explained by the 'belonging/ownership' facet: to be called by a name is to be claimed by its bearer (Num 6:27; Isa 43:7; 2 Chr 7:14), which does not require identifying the name with the covenant itself.","Phil 2:9-11 and Acts 4:12: the exalted name signifies the person and status of Jesus, awkward to paraphrase as 'no other covenant.'"],"book_explanatory_advantages":["The 2 Sam 7 dialogue substitution: David says 'the ark of God [of the covenant]' and God answers 'an house for my name' — the covenant reading makes the exchange a deliberate equation; the presence reading leaves the ark/name swap unexplained as anything more than coincidence.","Isa 4:1's actual bargain: the seven women waive the husband's covenant obligations of food and raiment (Ex 21:10) and ask only for the name — intelligible only if being 'called by thy name' is covenant standing; character/identity readings have nothing to do with the verse's mechanics.","Ruth 3:9's kanaph, cross-linked to Num 15:38-39 (commandment-tassels on the corners), Ruth 2:12 (wings of the LORD), Ezek 16:8 (God spreads His skirt and 'entered into a covenant'), and Zech 8:23 — a tight, multi-witness lattice binding name-taking, wing, and law that the printed entry summarizes exactly.","Ex 20:7 as 'bear the name for emptiness' explains Ezek 36:20-23 (name profaned by conduct, not speech) and Matt 7:21-23 (constant users of the name rejected as workers of lawlessness) in one stroke; the speech-focused reading must treat those as loosely related.","Deut 28:58 explicitly conditions fearing 'this glorious and fearful name' on doing 'all the words of this law,' and Rev 14:1, 12 pairs the Father's name on the forehead with keeping the commandments — the name-law-covenant binding is textual, not inferred.","Ex 6:3 (not known by my name JEHOVAH, though Abraham heard the word in Gen 15:7) is resolved without strain: knowing the name = entering what it carries, not learning a vocable."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Ex 34:5-7 and Ex 3:13-15 are more naturally read as the name disclosing God's character and being than as disclosing a covenant per se (though the disclosure is itself covenantal in context).","Phil 2:9-11 ('the name above every name') and personal naming scenes (Matt 1:21) fit 'name = person/status' more directly than 'name = covenant.'","Name theology for 2 Sam 7:13 / Deut 12 has substantial scholarly backing as divine presence rather than covenant."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["2 Samuel 7:2, 5, 13 — the ark-of-the-covenant / my-name substitution in the same dialogue","Isaiah 4:1 with Exodus 21:10 — 'called by thy name' as marriage, with the covenant obligations expressly waived","Ruth 3:9 with Ruth 2:12, Numbers 15:38-39, and Ezekiel 16:8 — the kanaph spread as covenant-marriage, its corners carrying the commandment-tassels","Exodus 20:7 with Ezekiel 36:20-23 and Matthew 7:21-23 — the name taken/profaned/invoked emptily by conduct, not sound","Deuteronomy 28:58 and Revelation 14:1, 12 — the name and the law bound together on the bearers","Exodus 6:3 with Genesis 15:7 — knowing the name as covenant-entry rather than vocabulary"],"unresolved_objections":["Character-proclamation texts (Ex 3:13-15; 34:5-7) and exaltation texts (Phil 2:9-11) remain more naturally read as name = the person's revealed being/status; the book's covenant reading may be the dominant metonymy for name-bearing texts rather than an exclusive definition of every 'name' occurrence.","The identification of the Angel of Exodus 23 as the pre-incarnate Christ is a secondary theological claim not required by the core and not adjudicated here.","The reading of Isaiah 4:1's seven women as the assemblies of God's people (via Rev 1:20's seven) is suggestive numerology, not demonstrated.","Deuteronomic name-theology (name as mode of divine presence in the temple) is not refuted, only outflanked; it remains a live scholarly account of 2 Sam 7:13 and Deut 12."],"confidence":"medium"}
